title: Square Systems: the Determinant Test
quickIdea: For n equations in n unknowns the determinant is a yes-or-no gate: non-zero means one solution and only one; zero means none or infinitely many, and you must look further to know which.
remember: If A is n x n and |A| is not 0, then rank(A) = n, so rank([A|b]) = n for every b and the system has exactly one solution.
If |A| = 0 then rank(A) < n, and the system has either no solution or infinitely many. It can never have exactly one, and it can never have exactly k solutions for a finite k above 1.
Which of the two it is depends on b: no solution when rank([A|b]) = rank(A) + 1, infinitely many when rank([A|b]) = rank(A).
A non-zero determinant is a property of A alone, so 'unique solution for every b' and '|A| is not 0' are the same statement.
A zero determinant is not a property of the system: the same singular A can be inconsistent for one b and have infinitely many solutions for another.

example.prompt: How many solutions has 2x1 - x2 + 3x3 = 1, 3x1 + 2x2 + 5x3 = 2, -x1 + 4x2 + x3 = 3?
example.work: The coefficient matrix is [[2,-1,3],[3,2,5],[-1,4,1]]. Expanding along the first row: 2(2 x 1 - 5 x 4) - (-1)(3 x 1 - 5 x (-1)) + 3(3 x 4 - 2 x (-1)) = 2(-18) + 1(8) + 3(14) = -36 + 8 + 42 = 14. The determinant is 14, which is not 0.
example.answer: Exactly one solution, because the determinant is non-zero. This is GATE CSE 2005 Q.48, whose answer is 'a unique solution'.

gateAngle: GATE uses the determinant as the fast route and the rank test as the general one. GATE CSE 2005 Q.48 is a pure determinant computation; GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 Q.13 is the trap in reverse, where the determinant is zero for two values of k and the two values behave differently; GATE CSE 2008 Q.3 asks for the parameter values that keep the determinant away from zero.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A is 3 x 3 with |A| = 0. Is it true that Ax = b has infinitely many solutions for every b?
variations.answer: No. It is true for some b and false for others.
variations.why: A zero determinant only removes the unique case. Consistency still has to be checked, and for most b a singular A is inconsistent.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why can a square system never have exactly two solutions?
variations.answer: Because the solution set is either empty or a coset of the null space of A, which contains 1 element (unique) or infinitely many.
variations.why: If x and y both solve Ax = b then x - y is in the null space, and every scalar multiple of x - y can be added to x to produce another solution.

trap.why: A zero determinant is consistent with both failures. The determinant is computed from A alone, while the number of solutions also depends on b.
trap.counterexample: A = [[1,1],[2,2]] has determinant 0. With b = (1,2) the equations are x + y = 1 and 2x + 2y = 2, the same line twice, so there are infinitely many solutions; with b = (1,3) they are x + y = 1 and 2x + 2y = 3, parallel lines, so there is none.

check.question: A is 4 x 4 with |A| = 0 and Ax = b is given. What are the possible numbers of solutions?
check.explanation: A zero determinant forces rank(A) below 4, so if the system is consistent at all there is at least one free parameter and hence infinitely many solutions.
